public_rationale: The October 20, 2026 Federal Register notice documents DeepSeek restrictions on federal civilian procurement and information technology [e1]. CRS stated on October 23 that the restrictions do not prohibit nongovernmental access or use; it raised possible indirect effects on private adoption without establishing them [e2]. These records do not establish the qualifying commercial-market barrier or its predicted effects, so the conditional forecast remains unresolved [e1, e2].
limitations: The documented restrictions do not establish that a qualifying barrier exists, but the packet does not prove that none exists.
The evidence provides no complete causal evaluation of prices, AI progress, benefits to OpenAI and Anthropic, or attributable harm to at least 200,000 other businesses.
Possible indirect commercial effects of procurement restrictions remain unmeasured.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: If the US builds a regulatory moat, it would certainly slow down progress and raise prices, helping two US companies at the expense of hundreds of thousands of others.
conditions: if the US builds a regulatory moat

statement.excerpt: Certainly it would slow down progress and raise prices, helping two US companies at the expense of hundreds of thousands of others.
statement.document_title: China has all but caught up. The US is not going to “win” the AI war. Here’s what we should do instead.

from_speaker: slow down progress and raise prices
at the expense of hundreds of thousands of others
our_interpretation: The condition is an implemented US barrier that materially restricts competing models in the commercial market to protect OpenAI and Anthropic. A proposal alone does not qualify.
The two beneficiaries are OpenAI and Anthropic. Progress means improvements in AI capabilities, products, and deployment; prices means prices paid by US AI customers for comparable services.
Hundreds of thousands means at least 200,000 other businesses suffering attributable harm. This numerical floor is my interpretation.
The claimed effects must result from the barrier, rather than merely follow it.
criteria.support_condition: After a qualifying barrier takes effect, credible causal evidence shows slower AI progress, higher comparable-service prices, benefits to both named labs, and harm to at least 200,000 other businesses.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A sufficiently complete evaluation of a qualifying policy episode establishes that one or more of the asserted effects did not occur. A short period without an observed effect is insufficient.

evidence.publisher: US Department of Homeland Security / Federal Register
evidence.explanation: This establishes a real DeepSeek restriction, but its stated scope is federal civilian procurement and information technology. It does not establish the commercial-market moat described in the contract or benefits concentrated in the two named labs.

evidence.locator: Considerations for Congress, paragraph beginning “The FASC limits federal procurement”
evidence.publisher: Congressional Research Service, reproduced by EveryCRSReport.com
evidence.explanation: CRS distinguishes the procurement restriction from restrictions on ordinary commercial access. Its accompanying discussion leaves possible indirect deterrence of private adoption as a question, rather than an established market-wide effect.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Official records establishing a qualifying implemented commercial-market barrier, followed by a sufficiently complete causal evaluation against a credible no-policy comparison. Support requires higher comparable-service prices, slower AI progress, benefits to both named labs, and harm to at least 200,000 other businesses; contradiction requires establishing that at least one asserted effect did not occur.
